title: My Ex-Husband’s New Wife Told Me to Pack After My Father’s Funeral—She Had No Idea What Was Waiting in the Will
excerpt: “START PACKING ALREADY, BECAUSE AS SOON AS THEY READ THE WILL TOMORROW, THIS HOUSE WILL BE OURS.”
author: admin

blocks.text: “START PACKING ALREADY, BECAUSE AS SOON AS THEY READ THE WILL TOMORROW, THIS HOUSE WILL BE OURS.”
Misty’s voice reached me over the white rose bushes before I even looked up.

Her thin heels sank into the damp garden soil like it was a runway, not the place where my father had spent half his life. She stood with one hand resting on her designer handbag and the other holding a pair of oversized sunglasses. Her perfectly curled blonde hair barely moved in the afternoon breeze.
I kept trimming the dry edges from a white rose.

I had buried my father only three days earlier. The black dress I wore to his funeral was still hanging over the back of a chair inside the house, and the scent of the lilies people had brought remained trapped in the hallway.
I hadn’t slept properly since the hospital called me.
And now my ex-husband’s new wife had arrived to tell me I was being thrown out of my own home.
“Don’t play games with me, Claire. You heard what I said.”
“Then why are you still standing there cutting flowers?”
She stared at me as if I had spoken another language.
“Your father is dead, Claire. The house is going to Daniel’s family. You need to start accepting reality.”
The man who had walked away from our marriage four years earlier after telling me that I was too ordinary for the life he wanted.
The man who had married Misty less than six months after our divorce was finalized.
The man who had once told me that my father was a stubborn old fool who would never amount to anything.
And now Misty was standing in my father’s garden, announcing that she intended to take his house.
I placed the pruning shears on the stone ledge.
“You seem very certain about what tomorrow’s will reading will say.”
“Oh, Claire. Please. Daniel has already explained everything to me.”
She stepped closer, careful not to let her expensive shoes touch the wet grass.
“Your father and Daniel had an arrangement. Everyone knows that. Daniel helped him with business matters for years. Your father promised him this property. The house, the land, everything.”

My father had built it with his own hands over thirty years ago, adding the porch one summer and planting the garden the next. Every brick held a memory. Every window had been chosen by him. The white roses had come from my mother’s original garden.
My father had kept them alive long after she died.
He used to say they were the only things in the world that could make him feel young again.
And Misty believed she could claim all of it because her husband had told her a story.
“Did Daniel tell you that himself?” I asked.
For the first time, her expression flickered.
I smiled faintly and returned to the roses.
She believed my silence meant I was frightened.
And most importantly, she believed that because I was no longer married to Daniel, I had no place in the story of my father’s estate.
She had absolutely no idea what my father had spent the last six months preparing.
Or why he had made me promise that no matter what happened, I would let the lawyers read every word of his will before I reacted to anything.
Especially if Daniel came looking for the house.
Because my father had known something about my ex-husband that I had spent years trying to ignore.
Daniel had never stopped wanting what belonged to someone else.
And tomorrow, he was going to discover that wanting something and owning it were two very different things.
Four years earlier, Daniel and I had divorced in a courthouse that smelled of old paper and floor polish.
For most of that time, I believed we were happy.
We lived in a modest house outside town. I worked as an accountant for a local construction company, while Daniel moved between business ventures, always chasing the next opportunity.
Whenever he lost money, I helped him recover. I paid our mortgage when his business failed. I sold jewelry my mother had left me when he needed capital for a new investment.
And when he became embarrassed by his failures, I told everyone we were doing fine.
My father never believed Daniel’s excuses.
“Claire,” he told me one evening, sitting at his kitchen table, “a man who respects you will never ask you to keep shrinking so he can feel tall.”
“Everyone is under pressure. It doesn’t give them permission to become cruel.”
I defended him when he criticized my clothes.
I defended him when he complained that I spent too much time visiting my father.
I even defended him when he began referring to my father’s house as an investment opportunity.
That was the first time I saw the greed beneath his charm.
My father owned twelve acres of land outside town. Over the decades, the surrounding area had grown, and developers had begun purchasing nearby properties.
The land was worth far more than it had been when my father bought it.
He began suggesting that my father sell the property and move into a retirement community.
“He could live comfortably,” Daniel said. “And we’d help him manage the money.”
Daniel never forgave him for that answer.

After our divorce, Daniel moved into a luxury apartment downtown. Within months, he appeared in photographs beside Misty, a real estate agent who had once worked with him on a commercial property deal.
She was younger than me, beautiful, and extraordinarily good at making ordinary things look expensive.

He loved being photographed in restaurants he couldn’t afford without borrowing money. He loved talking about investments he hadn’t secured. He loved telling people that his future was going to be bigger than their imagination.
Together, they built a life out of promises.
And then, three days after my father’s funeral, she came to collect a house she believed was already hers.
My father, Thomas Bennett, had been eighty-one when he died.
